summary: Specifies the frame format, maximum transmission unit and address assignment procedures for sending IPv4 packets over the IP-specific Packet Convergence Sublayer of IEEE 802.16 wireless broadband. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: The instructions for fitting internet packets into the wireless boxes used by a certain broadband radio system.

questions: what is the ipv4 convergence sublayer
what is the default mtu for ipv4 over 802.16
how do hosts get ipv4 addresses over wimax
subtitle: How IPv4 packets ride directly inside IEEE 802.16 (WiMAX) frames, with a default MTU of 1500 and DHCP for addresses.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.16 wireless broadband can carry IPv4 directly through its IP-specific Packet Convergence Sublayer, but IP hosts needed rules for the frame format, the MTU and address assignment.
tldr.mechanism: IPv4 packets go in the payload of generic 802.16 MAC frames over a point-to-point link between each host and its access router. The default MTU SHOULD be 1500 octets, and DHCP SHOULD assign each host a /32 address.
tldr.outcome: Hosts get a simple per-host IPv4 link with no ARP, but a mismatch with deployments that use a smaller MTU can silently drop packets.

today: RFC 5948 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope and Terminology
sections.content:
IEEE 802.16 is a connection-oriented access technology for the last mile, the final leg of connectivity from a provider to a customer. Its MAC layer has several Convergence Sublayers (CSs) for carrying higher-layer packets. This RFC covers only the IP-specific part of the Packet CS, which it calls the IPv4 CS.

The document specifies how to encapsulate and send IPv4 packets over the IPv4 CS, plus the MTU and the address assignment method. It uses MS (Mobile Station) informally to mean the whole IP host, not just the 802.16 interface. Other terms follow RFC 5154.
sections.eli5: Wireless broadband has several ways to wrap up data. This document explains just one of them, the one made for internet packets, and covers how to wrap them, how big they can be and how a computer gets its address.

sections.title: Network Architecture and the IPv4 CS Link
sections.content:
The architecture follows RFC 5154 and RFC 5121. Each MS attaches to an Access Router (AR) through a Base Station (BS), which is a Layer 2 entity from the point of view of the IPv4 link.

In 802.16 the transport connection between MS and BS carries user data, and a transport connection is represented by a service flow. An MS can have several. When the AR and BS are co-located, the set of transport connections to an MS is a single IPv4 link. When they are separate, a tunnel SHOULD be set up between them, with granularity no greater than per MS or per service flow, and the tunnels plus transport connections form one point-to-point IPv4 link.

Each host sits on its own IPv4 link and gets a unique IPv4 address, similar to the model discussed in RFC 4968. Link establishment follows Section 6.2 of RFC 5121: step 5 indicates IPv4 support, and step 6 creates a service flow for IP-layer signaling such as DHCP.
sections.eli5: Your computer talks to a radio tower, and the tower hands the data to a router. Each computer gets its own private line to the router, so it never shares a hallway with other computers.

sections.title: The MAC Frame for IPv4 Packets
sections.content:
IPv4 packets travel in generic 802.16 MAC frames, inside the data payload of the 802.16 PDU. The frame starts with a MAC header, then the IPv4 header and payload, then an optional CRC.

Key header fields: H (header type, set to zero for a Generic MAC PDU), E (1 means the payload is encrypted), C (1 means a CRC is included), LEN (11 bits, the length in bytes of the whole MAC PDU including header and any CRC), CID (the 16-bit connection identifier) and HCS (an 8-bit header check sequence). The TYPE field says which subheaders and special payload types are present. The CRC is an optional 8-bit field appended after encryption.
sections.eli5: Each packet goes into an envelope with a label on the front. The label says how long the letter is, which private line it belongs on and whether it is scrambled.

sections.title: The Maximum Transmission Unit
sections.content:
The MTU for IPv4 on an 802.16 link is configurable, and the default SHOULD be 1500 octets. RFC 5121 notes the IP MTU can be larger or smaller. The problem is that if an MS sends 1500-octet packets in a deployment with a smaller MTU, packets may be dropped silently at the link layer. IPv6 can advertise the MTU in Neighbor Discovery, but IPv4 has no similarly reliable mechanism, because legacy IPv4 clients do not determine the link MTU before sending.

Ways to learn the MTU:

  • The 2009 revision of IEEE 802.16 can provide the MAC MTU in the SBC-REQ/SBC-RSP phase. This only helps when the MS is directly connected to the BS, and the implementation must pass the value up to the IP layer.
  • The DHCP interface MTU option from RFC 2132. IPv4 and IPv4 CS clients SHOULD use it to set their interface MTU.

Without DHCP MTU configuration, the MS can use the default 1500 or use the 802.16-2009 methods. Clients are also encouraged to run Path MTU Discovery (RFC 1191) or PLPMTUD (RFC 4821), though PMTU has its own problems when ICMP messages do not reach the sender or when the Don't Fragment bit is set and routers do not fragment.
sections.eli5: The MTU is the biggest box that fits through the pipe. If you send a box that is too big for a narrow pipe, it may just vanish without a word. So the computer should ask how big a box is allowed.

sections.title: Subnet Model and Address Assignment
sections.content:
The recommended subnet model is a point-to-point link between the MS and the AR (as in RFC 4968), so each MS is assigned an address with a 32-bit prefix length or subnet mask. The link is built from 802.16 MAC connections (service flows) plus an L2 tunnel such as GRE between the BS and the AR, unless the AR and BS are co-located. The next hop for an MS is always the AR.

DHCP SHOULD assign the IPv4 address. DHCP messages are carried over the 802.16 MAC connection and relayed to the AR. If the DHCP server is not in the AR, the AR SHOULD implement a DHCP relay agent (RFC 1542).

The IPv4 CS does not allow ARP (RFC 826) packets, and on a point-to-point link address resolution is not needed. Broadcast and multicast packets from the MS reach the AR over the point-to-point link. The RFC assumes those services exist and leaves their implementation out of scope.
sections.eli5: Because each computer has its own private line to the router, every computer gets an address that is only for itself. Nobody has to shout "who has this address?" down a shared hallway.

sections.title: How Packets Are Sent and Received
sections.content:
Appendix B explains the flow. Before any packet moves, an 802.16 transport connection must exist: a MAC connection between MS and BS, plus an L2 tunnel between BS and AR if they are separate. All packets from the MS reach the AR before going on to their destination.

The IPv4 CS classifies each packet by upper-layer header fields to pick a connection (CID). The classifiers are source and destination IPv4 addresses, source and destination ports, Type-of-Service and the IP Protocol field. The CS may use Packet Header Suppression (PHS) afterwards, and the BS optionally rebuilds the header. The AR does normal routing, but its DHCP relay agent MUST keep track of the tunnel interface on which it got each DHCP request so replies reach the right MS.

Appendix A adds that an MS using only the Ethernet CS and one using only the IPv4 CS cannot talk at the data link layer. They need IP-layer interworking and must be on different subnets.
sections.eli5: The tower sorts each packet onto the right private line by reading its address label. The router then sends it on its way like a normal mail sorter.

sections.title: The WiMAX 1400-Octet MTU Conflict
sections.content:
Appendix C notes that the WiMAX Forum has specified its own IPv4 CS, which is similar to this specification. One significant difference is that WiMAX specifies the IP MTU as 1400 octets, not 1500. An MS configured for 1500 that enters a WiMAX network may run into the problems described above, and an IPv4 CS client cannot probe with ARP to find the link MTU.

The RFC says an MS should be able to sense that it is on a WiMAX network, for example from its authentication and network entry procedures, and adjust. It admits this is imperfect, and still recommends a default of 1500. That reflects the working group's consensus after much debate about the best value from the IETF's point of view.
sections.eli5: Two rulebooks disagree about the biggest box size: 1500 or 1400. The authors picked 1500 but warn that computers visiting a 1400 network need to notice and shrink their boxes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it introduces no new vulnerabilities to IPv4 specifications or operation. Air-interface security belongs to the IEEE 802.16 standard, and security issues in network architecture beyond the base stations belong to the documents defining those architectures, such as the WiMAX network architecture.
sections.eli5: This document adds no new security holes. Locking the radio link is the job of other rulebooks.
